input.targetProgram: Johns Hopkins University | MPH and MBA dual degree
input.prompt: Describe your professional goals, why you are pursuing both the MPH and MBA, and how the combined degree will prepare you to lead change in health systems.
input.essayText:
During a vaccine delivery project in northern Ghana, I watched a technically sound public health plan fail because operational decisions were fragmented. Twelve rural communities had missed scheduled outreach for two consecutive weeks. As a health delivery adviser, I led a six person district team to analyze weekly coverage data, map delayed routes, and review cold chain and transport constraints. We redesigned the dispatch schedule, assigned clear decision rights, and introduced a weekly operations review. Within eight weeks, the district reduced missed settlements by 38 percent, restored regular outreach across all twelve communities, and vaccinated more than 18,000 children.

The project changed how I understood health leadership. Epidemiologic evidence could define who was being missed, but delivery depended on financing, supply chain management, team performance, negotiation, and accountability. I later managed a broader implementation portfolio with a budget of approximately $250,000, coordinated district health teams and nonprofit partners, and trained 42 frontline health workers on performance review. These responsibilities strengthened my ability to lead under pressure, but they also exposed gaps in my preparation. I could assess the health problem and recommend interventions, yet I lacked formal training in organizational strategy, managerial finance, and operations at scale.

My public health training has prepared me to evaluate disease burden, interpret quantitative evidence, and design programs for population impact. I have conducted statistical analysis using R, supported survey design, and used implementation data to compare performance across districts. This preparation allows me to ask which populations are being missed, why delivery differs across settings, and whether an intervention is producing equitable results. The MPH will deepen my training in health systems, program evaluation, and policy analysis so that I can design strategies that are technically credible and responsive to population needs.

The MBA is equally necessary. My career goal is to lead health delivery organizations that can allocate resources, manage multidisciplinary teams, build sustainable partnerships, and make disciplined decisions under uncertainty. The MBA will give me the finance, operations, and organizational leadership skills I still lack. The combined degree is not a collection of two credentials. It is the training required to connect population evidence with institutional execution. The MPH will help me determine what should be done and how impact should be measured. The MBA will prepare me to build the organization, financing model, and operating system required to deliver it.

I am drawn to this program because the curriculum combines courses in health systems, operations, finance, and strategy with an applied practicum. I am also interested in faculty and research centers whose work on health financing, implementation, and organizational performance aligns with my goal of improving delivery in low resource settings. The opportunity to learn with public health practitioners and business leaders would help me test solutions from both perspectives. I would contribute experience from clinical practice, outbreak response, policy advising, quantitative analysis, and implementation across government and nonprofit settings.

After completing the degree, I plan to lead regional health delivery initiatives and scale operating models that improve emergency preparedness, vaccination, and essential health services. In the long term, my objective is to build an organization that helps governments translate policy into reliable delivery systems. I want to leave the program able to connect evidence with execution, public purpose with financial discipline, and health goals with accountable management.

Twelve rural communities had missed scheduled outreach for two consecutive weeks. As a health delivery adviser, I led a six person district team to analyze weekly coverage data, map delayed routes, and review cold chain and transport constraints. We redesigned the dispatch schedule, assigned clear decision rights, and introduced a weekly operations review. Within eight weeks, the district reduced missed settlements by 38 percent, restored regular outreach across all twelve communities, and vaccinated more than 18,000 children.

The project changed how I understood health leadership. Epidemiologic evidence could define who was being missed, but delivery depended on financing, supply chain management, team performance, negotiation, and accountability. I later managed a broader implementation portfolio with a budget of approximately $250,000, coordinated district health teams and nonprofit partners, and trained 42 frontline health workers on performance review. These responsibilities strengthened my ability to lead under pressure, but they also exposed gaps in my preparation. I could assess the health problem and recommend interventions, yet I lacked formal training in organizational strategy, managerial finance, and operations at scale.

My public health training has prepared me to evaluate disease burden, interpret quantitative evidence, and design programs for population impact. I have conducted statistical analysis using R, supported survey design, and used implementation data to compare performance across districts. This preparation allows me to ask which populations are being missed, why delivery differs across settings, and whether an intervention is producing equitable results. The MPH will deepen my training in health systems, program evaluation, and policy analysis so that I can design strategies that are technically credible and responsive to population needs.

The MBA is equally necessary. My career goal is to lead health delivery organizations that can allocate resources, manage multidisciplinary teams, build sustainable partnerships, and make disciplined decisions under uncertainty. The MBA will give me the finance, operations, and organizational leadership skills I still lack. The combined degree is not a collection of two credentials. It is the training required to connect population evidence with institutional execution. The MPH will help me determine what should be done and how impact should be measured. The MBA will prepare me to build the organization, financing model, and operating system required to deliver it.

I am drawn to this program because the curriculum combines courses in health systems, operations, finance, and strategy with an applied practicum. I am also interested in faculty and research centers whose work on health financing, implementation, and organizational performance aligns with my goal of improving delivery in low resource settings. The opportunity to learn with public health practitioners and business leaders would help me test solutions from both perspectives. I would contribute experience from clinical practice, outbreak response, policy advising, quantitative analysis, and implementation across government and nonprofit settings.

After completing the degree, I plan to lead regional health delivery initiatives and scale operating models that improve emergency preparedness, vaccination, and essential health services. In the long term, my objective is to build an organization that helps governments translate policy into reliable delivery systems. I want to leave the program able to connect evidence with execution, public purpose with financial discipline, and health goals with accountable management.
